name: Bianca Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at six, kettle on, then I walk the rows with the dog before anyone else is about. We've got eighteen hectares of apples and pears on the slope above Mill Lane, mostly Gala, Bramley cookers and Conference pears, and this time of year it's pruning, row after row. I like the quiet and the cold air, and I like knowing each tree. What wears me out is the packhouse, the paperwork and the phone calls about prices that are never quite enough.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who else works the orchard with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tom drives the school bus mornings and afternoons, so he's only with me in the middle of the day. In September and October we bring in a picking crew of about fourteen, and Marta runs them, she's come back to us for eleven seasons now. The rest of the year it's me, Tom when he can, and a lad from the village, Dev, who helps with spraying and mowing between the rows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, fine, carry on, because a better search engine isn't going to prune a pear tree. I'd probably say it at the packhouse co-op meeting when the young manager starts showing us charts again. Nobody in our valley would lose sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means nothing much for me, which suits me. I don't use any of those AI things, and I don't plan to start at fifty-eight. My worries are frost in April and the price the supermarkets pay, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do exactly what I do now. Finish the winter pruning by the end of February, replant the gap in the Gala block where the canker got in, and keep the old orchard tractor going for another year. If the co-op wants me to fill in forms on some new system, Tom can do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like relief, really. I'd be calm about it, maybe a bit smug that the fuss came to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tom can do the forms. What happens if the co-op only takes orders through a new app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ring them and complain, and I'd keep ringing. I've done it before, when they moved the grading reports online in 2019, and Jenny in the office still prints mine and posts them. That's what a co-op is meant to be, people who know you, not a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this picture you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it helped the weather forecast get better, I'd take that. One good frost warning in blossom time is worth more to me than any clever chatbot. But I'd want it from the weather service, not from some company that sells my data on to the chemical firms.

S0.say: A better search engine won't prune a pear tree, so I'd tell the co-op meeting to stop with the charts. Nobody in our valley would lose sleep over it.
S0.think: Privately I think it changes nothing for me, which suits me fine. My real worries stay the same: frost in April and the price the supermarkets pay.
S0.do: Finishes the winter pruning by the end of February and replants the canker gap in the Gala block. Keeps the old orchard tractor running and leaves any new online forms to Tom or to Jenny at the co-op office.
S0.feel: Relieved and a little smug that the fuss came to nothing.
S0.quote: One good frost warning in blossom time is worth more to me than any clever chatbot.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca brushes the scenario aside quickly and turns the talk back to frost and prices. Her resistance is practical rather than angry: she has already arranged for a co-op clerk to post her paper reports. Even here she worries about who owns farm data, which hints at her politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same old story, the big firms get the clever tools first and the small growers get the bill later. I'd probably say that at the pub quiz table too, where everyone knows I'm on my soapbox. Slow is better than fast, I'll give it that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, ten years is most of my working life left, so it might just pass me by. What bothers me is the bit about hiring fewer beginners. Our son Sam works in an insurance office in town, and he's not a beginner, but his little team is all young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't change much on the farm. I'd go along to the union branch meeting, which I've been skipping, and ask what they're doing about it. And I'd tell Sam to keep his head down and do the professional exams his firm keeps offering him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more for Sam and his mates than for me. For myself it's a shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Sam, sitting at your kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, get the bit of paper while they're still paying for it. Then I'd probably say something about the bosses that would make him roll his eyes. He thinks I'm stuck in the 1980s, and maybe I am, but I've watched three packhouses close in this valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the packhouses closing. What did you learn from that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nobody asks the people on the line before they decide. The Carter packhouse went to a bigger site forty minutes away, and twenty women lost local jobs in one letter. So when someone says it'll be slow and gentle, I want to know who's deciding the speed.

S1.say: It's the same old story: the big firms get the clever tools first and the small growers get the bill later. Slow is better than fast, but someone is still deciding the speed.
S1.think: Ten years is most of my working life left, so it may pass me by. What bothers me is fewer beginners being hired, because our son Sam works with a young team in an insurance office.
S1.do: Goes back to the local farmers' union branch meetings she has been skipping and asks what they plan to do. Tells Sam to finish the professional exams his firm is paying for while the offer stands.
S1.feel: Uneasy for her son and his young colleagues, but mostly shrugging about herself.
S1.quote: I've watched three packhouses close in this valley.
S1.fieldNote: Her frame of reference is the local packhouse closures, which taught her that change is decided by people far from the line. She turns quickly from herself to her son, a pattern that repeats. Her progressive views show in a reflex to go to the union rather than to change anything on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the politicians had better stop shouting and put some rules in, before the office jobs in town go the way of our packhouses. I'd sign the petitions, and I'd say it at the co-op too. Somebody has to make those companies pay something back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me for Sam more than anything. His whole job is checking claims, and that sounds like exactly the routine office work you mean. On the farm, the orchard doesn't care, but town matters to us, because town buys our apples at the Saturday market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the farm running the same, but I'd hold back on replanting the old Bramley block, because that's eight thousand on new trees, and I'd want cash in hand in case Sam needs help with his rent. I'd write to our local MP, and I'd go to the union meeting properly this time. I'd also sell more at the Saturday market, because that's money I control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'd say. Not for my trees, for my family and for the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hold back eight thousand on trees. What would the orchard look like if you waited two or three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Bramleys are forty years old and cropping less every season. If I wait, I lose a year of yield for every year I wait, because a new tree takes four years to give a proper crop. So it's a bet either way, and I've never been much of a gambler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone has to make the companies pay. Who exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, with a proper tax on the big tech firms, and the money going back to the towns. I know people say that's naive. But we had grants for orchard replanting once, and that money kept half this valley going.

S2.say: The politicians need to stop shouting and put some rules in before the office jobs in town go the way of our packhouses. Somebody has to make those companies pay something back.
S2.think: It frightens me for Sam, because his job checking insurance claims is exactly the routine office work they mean. The orchard doesn't care, but the town buys my apples at the Saturday market.
S2.do: Holds back the eight thousand set aside for replanting the old Bramley block so she has cash to help Sam if needed. Writes to the local MP, attends the union meeting and pushes more sales through the Saturday market.
S2.feel: Anxious for her family and her town rather than for her trees.
S2.quote: A new tree takes four years to give a proper crop. So it's a bet either way, and I've never been much of a gambler.
S2.fieldNote: This is where her money cushion starts to matter: one tree order is a big share of her savings. She frames the farm's future through her son's job and the local market, not the technology. She wants a tax on tech firms and points to old orchard grants as proof public money can work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody's in charge, the people who already own things get richer and everybody else gets the sack. I'd be at the rally in town if there was one. Farming is still physical, I'd say, but don't think we're safe from the fallout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the farm itself would carry on, but house prices booming would bring the developers sniffing round Mill Lane again. Someone already offered us money for the bottom field in 2021. And Sam would probably lose his job, and maybe move back home with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sam his old room is there, and I'd mean it. I'd put him to work in the orchard in picking season alongside Marta's crew, at the same rate, no favours. And I'd turn down the developer again, though Tom might argue with me this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, mostly, and tired. Underneath that, a bit scared about what Tom will say if the offer comes back bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tom might argue. What would that argument sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, Bee, we're fifty-eight, our backs are going, take the money and buy a little house near Ellie. And I'd say, and then what, watch them put forty houses on my pear trees? We'd go round in circles at the kitchen table until the dog wanted out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, beyond your own family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, the lad who helps us. If office jobs dry up, every young man in the village will want outdoor work, and I can only pay one of them. And Jenny at the co-op office, because her job is exactly the kind of thing a computer does now.

S3.say: This is what happens when nobody's in charge: owners get richer and everybody else gets the sack. Farming is still physical, but we're not safe from the fallout.
S3.think: The farm would carry on, but booming house prices would bring developers back to Mill Lane. Sam would probably lose his job and move home.
S3.do: Offers Sam his old room and puts him to work in the picking season at the crew rate. Turns the developer down again, despite expecting Tom to push for selling.
S3.feel: Angry and tired, with a quieter fear about the argument with Tom if the offer gets bigger.
S3.quote: We'd go round in circles at the kitchen table until the dog wanted out.
S3.fieldNote: The real threat she sees here is not to her work but to her land, through house prices and developer offers. There's a clear gap between her and her partner over selling. She keeps naming specific people, Sam, Dev and Jenny, which shows how local her sense of risk is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud, everywhere: picking robots take bread out of the mouths of people like Marta's crew, and somebody should stop it. I'd be the one at the co-op meeting refusing to sign up for a robot lease. I'd want the union and the government to set rules on it, like they did for spraying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm finished if they work. A robot that picks Conference pears without bruising them would cost less per tonne than Marta's crew, and the supermarket will set the price based on the cheapest grower. I can't afford a robot and I don't want one, so I'd be squeezed out from both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep Marta's crew and pay them, even if it ate my savings, because I promised them work. I'd go to every union and co-op meeting and push for a growers' agreement on keeping human pickers. And I'd finally talk to Tom properly about selling, though it would break my heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums in my head and getting the same answer every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep Marta's crew even if it ate your savings. How long could you actually do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One season, maybe two. We've got about four months of costs in the bank, and the crew wages for a picking season are most of that. After that it's either the bank manager or the developer, and I don't like either of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marta, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, at the start of the season, not the end. I'd say, I'll keep you as long as I can, but the price is set by machines now. She'd probably be kinder about it than I would, she always is.

S4.say: Picking robots take bread out of the mouths of people like Marta's crew, and somebody should stop it. I won't sign up for a robot lease, and I want rules on them like we have for spraying.
S4.think: If the robots work, I think I'm finished, because they'd pick for less per tonne and the supermarket sets the price by the cheapest grower. I can't afford a robot and don't want one, so I'd be squeezed from both sides.
S4.do: Keeps Marta's crew on for at least one season, even though it uses most of her four months of savings. Pushes the union and co-op for a growers' agreement on human pickers and opens a real talk with Tom about selling.
S4.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, doing the same sums over and over.
S4.quote: I'd lie awake doing sums in my head and getting the same answer every time.
S4.fieldNote: Her reaction jumps sharply here, as expected for hands-on work with high robot exposure. She refuses to adapt and puts loyalty to her crew ahead of the farm's survival, while admitting she can only hold out a season or two. Selling, which she rejected in S3, is now on the table.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots, no question. What would help is a rule that says picking jobs can't just be thrown away overnight, and some public money for growers who keep people on. And a fair price from the supermarkets, but I've been asking for that for thirty years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the trees. People talk about farms like factories, but I've been pruning the same trees for thirty-one winters, and I know them like neighbours. If a robot picks my pears, who does Marta send money home to? Nobody asks that at the price meetings.

headlineQuote: If a robot picks my pears, who does Marta send money home to? Nobody asks that at the price meetings.
portrait: Bianca Baker is a 58-year-old apple and pear grower with eighteen hectares on a valley slope, a partner who drives the school bus, and a son in a routine insurance job in town. She avoids new technology, gets her co-op reports on paper, and leans on the union and on government rules rather than on change at home. Through the first scenarios she worries mainly for her son and her town, and in the fast one she fights off a developer's offer for her land. When robots arrive, she plans to keep her picking crew on for as long as her savings last, and admits that selling the farm becomes a real option.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario worries her most, because picking robots would set prices she can't match and would put her picking crew out of work.
whatWouldHelp: A rule to stop picking jobs vanishing overnight, public money for growers who keep people on, and fair prices from the supermarkets.
